name: Payment Gateway (Stripe-like)
description: Design a payment gateway like Stripe. Covers idempotent charge creation, async bank processing, webhook delivery, PCI compliance, and exactly-once payment guarantees.

learnSteps.title: Idempotent Charge Creation
learnSteps.description: Merchants send charge requests with an idempotency key (UUID) to the API Gateway. The Payment Service checks PostgreSQL for an existing charge with that key. If found, it returns the cached result (idempotent retry). If not, it creates a new charge record with status PENDING in a serializable transaction. This prevents duplicate charges from network retries. The API Gateway enforces per-merchant rate limits and API key authentication.

learnSteps.title: Async Payment Processing
learnSteps.description: After creating a PENDING charge, the Payment Service publishes a process event to Kafka and returns a 202 Accepted. The Payment Processor Worker consumes the event and calls the bank/card network API (Visa, Mastercard, ACH). Bank APIs have ~800ms latency and ~3% error rate. This async pattern decouples the fast API response from slow bank processing, preventing client timeouts on long-running bank calls.

learnSteps.title: Bank Integration and Settlement
learnSteps.description: The Worker sends the charge to the bank API with transaction details. On success, it updates the Ledger DB to SUCCEEDED and creates double-entry accounting records (debit merchant, credit platform). On failure, it marks FAILED and triggers retry with exponential backoff (up to 5 attempts). Bank declines are terminal and not retried. The Worker uses distributed locks to prevent concurrent processing of the same charge.

learnSteps.title: Exactly-Once Processing and Audit Trail
learnSteps.description: The system achieves exactly-once semantics through idempotency keys at the API level and transactional outbox pattern at the DB level. Every state transition is logged in an immutable audit table. Kafka retains events for 30 days for replay and reconciliation. Daily batch reconciliation compares the ledger against bank settlement files to detect discrepancies. PCI compliance is achieved by tokenizing card data before it reaches the Payment Service.

chaosScenarios.name: Bank Network Brownout
chaosScenarios.description: Acquirer authorization latency rises from ~800ms to 5-8s with elevated declines
chaosScenarios.expectedBehavior: The 60 in-flight worker slots (6 instances x 10 concurrency) saturate; Kafka backlog grows and charges sit PENDING for minutes. The synchronous API path is unaffected — merchants still get 202s — but confirmation-sensitive merchants see delayed outcomes.
mitigationSteps: Cut the per-call timeout to 3s and stop retrying timeouts immediately — retries amplify brownouts
Open the acquirer circuit breaker and route eligible card types to a backup acquirer
Scale workers on consumer lag to absorb the backlog once the bank recovers
Publish degraded-processing status to merchant dashboards

chaosScenarios.name: Ledger Primary Failure
chaosScenarios.description: The PostgreSQL ledger primary crashes, forcing replica promotion
chaosScenarios.expectedBehavior: Charge creation returns 5xx (no ledger record means no 202) and workers cannot commit state transitions, so all money movement halts. Failover takes 30-60s; in-flight bank calls complete but their results queue against the new primary.
mitigationSteps: Promote the synchronous replica; verify zero replication lag before accepting writes
Let workers replay in-flight events — idempotency keys and per-charge locks prevent double-charging
Run targeted reconciliation against bank records for every charge mid-flight during failover
Hold merchant webhooks until ledger state is verified consistent

chaosScenarios.name: Kafka Broker Loss and Consumer Rebalance
chaosScenarios.description: A broker drops; partitions reassign and the payment consumer group rebalances, redelivering in-flight events
chaosScenarios.expectedBehavior: Replication factor 3 keeps partitions available, but in-flight events are redelivered to new consumers. The duplicate-suppression path (idempotency keys plus per-charge locks) is exercised under load, and processing p99 spikes for 1-2 minutes during the rebalance pause.
mitigationSteps: Verify all partitions retained an in-sync replica
Audit the ledger transition log to confirm no charge reached SUCCEEDED twice
Use static consumer-group membership and cooperative rebalancing to shrink pause windows
Alert if the duplicate-suppression hit rate spikes — it indicates a redelivery storm

bottleneckProgression.description: At ~800ms per bank call, the 60 in-flight slots cap processing near 75 charges/s; Kafka lag grows beyond that
bottleneckProgression.resolution: Scale workers horizontally or raise per-instance concurrency — until the acquirer rate limit becomes the ceiling

bottleneckProgression.description: The contracted 1000 RPS acquirer limit becomes the hard ceiling regardless of worker count
bottleneckProgression.resolution: Add a second acquirer with traffic splitting, or negotiate a higher rate tier

bottleneckProgression.description: Serializable idempotency-key inserts and double-entry writes saturate the 300-connection ledger pool
bottleneckProgression.resolution: Front the pool with pgbouncer, batch ledger entries per transaction, and partition hot merchants

expectedIssues.title: Charges Stuck in PENDING
expectedIssues.description: A worker that dies after the bank call but before the ledger update leaves a charge PENDING with money actually moved
expectedIssues.mitigation: A sweeper re-queries the bank by gateway reference for any charge PENDING beyond 5 minutes; daily reconciliation against settlement files catches the rest

expectedIssues.title: Idempotency Key Insert Races
expectedIssues.description: Two concurrent retries with the same key can both pass a read-then-write existence check before either inserts
expectedIssues.mitigation: A unique constraint on idempotency_key with INSERT ... ON CONFLICT is the single source of truth — never a read-then-write check

expectedIssues.title: Retry Amplification Against a Degraded Bank
expectedIssues.description: Up to five retry attempts per charge multiply load exactly when the acquirer is least able to handle it
expectedIssues.mitigation: Exponential backoff with jitter, a global retry budget, and circuit breaking; hard declines are terminal and never retried

expectedIssues.title: Single Ledger Write Primary
expectedIssues.description: Every money movement serializes through one PostgreSQL primary; its write throughput and failover behavior bound the whole platform
expectedIssues.mitigation: Partition the ledger by merchant ID when write volume demands it, and keep failover drills on a regular schedule

steps: Check acquirer status and the decline-code distribution (issuer vs network errors)
Drop timeouts to 3s and pause automatic retries
Fail over eligible traffic to the secondary acquirer
Communicate processing delays to merchants and reconcile once recovered
Query for charges PENDING beyond 5 minutes
Re-query the bank by gateway reference to learn the true outcome
Transition ledger state idempotently — never guess an outcome
If volume is large, run bulk reconciliation and notify finance
Freeze processing for the affected merchant
Audit the ledger for duplicate idempotency keys and double SUCCEEDED transitions
Refund confirmed duplicates within the same business day
Root-cause the idempotency gap before unfreezing

decisions.title: Asynchronous Processing With Synchronous Acknowledgement
decisions.context: Bank authorization takes ~800ms with a ~3% error rate; holding client connections open couples merchant latency to acquirer health
decisions.decision: Persist the charge as PENDING, return 202 immediately, and process via Kafka workers
consequences: API latency is independent of bank latency
Merchants must handle an asynchronous completion model (polling or webhooks)
A backlog can form between acceptance and completion that needs its own SLO

decisions.title: Idempotency Keys + Transactional State Machine
decisions.context: Network retries are routine, and a duplicate charge is the worst failure mode in payments
decisions.decision: Merchant-supplied idempotency keys enforced by a unique constraint; all charge state transitions run in serializable transactions
consequences: Retries are safe from both merchants and internal workers
Write contention on the ledger is higher than with looser isolation
Exactly-once effects are achieved on top of at-least-once delivery

decisions.title: Double-Entry Ledger in PostgreSQL
decisions.context: Financial state must be auditable and always balance to zero
decisions.decision: Every movement writes balanced debit/credit rows to an append-only ledger with an immutable audit table
consequences: Reconciliation against bank settlement files is mechanical
Write throughput is bounded by a single primary
Mutable balance shortcuts are forbidden by construction

tradeoffs.benefit: The API stays fast and available through acquirer brownouts
tradeoffs.cost: Merchants wait seconds — occasionally minutes — for the terminal charge state

tradeoffs.benefit: No double-spend or unbalanced entries under concurrency
tradeoffs.cost: The ledger primary caps peak charge throughput

tradeoffs.benefit: Any consumer bug can be replayed weeks later for reconciliation
tradeoffs.cost: Meaningful broker storage spend relative to event volume

alternatives.name: Fully Synchronous Charge API
alternatives.description: Hold the client connection open through bank authorization
alternatives.prosVsCons: Simplest merchant integration — one call, one answer — but p99 inherits bank tail latency and timeouts create ambiguous outcomes that breed duplicate retries
alternatives.whyNotChosen: Ambiguous timeout states are unacceptable in money movement

alternatives.name: Event-Sourced Ledger
alternatives.description: Store all state as an event log and derive balances by projection
alternatives.prosVsCons: Perfect audit trail and temporal queries, but projection lag complicates current-balance reads and tooling maturity is lower
alternatives.whyNotChosen: A double-entry relational ledger achieves auditability with simpler operational semantics

alternatives.name: Saga Orchestration Service
alternatives.description: A central orchestrator coordinating each charge workflow step
alternatives.prosVsCons: Explicit workflow visibility, but adds another stateful service in the money path
alternatives.whyNotChosen: A single bank call per charge does not justify orchestration overhead; Kafka plus idempotent workers suffice
